text: Name a person with an ML or stats concept named after them
note: Type the surname, e.g. Bayes. Anyone whose name is on a theorem, distribution, test, algorithm, metric or method used in ML or statistics

answers.q: A South African mining engineer estimating gold grades. Kriging is Gaussian process regression with a hard hat.
Karl's son. The Pearson in Neyman–Pearson.
The Schwarz criterion, better known as BIC.
Found the normal curve in 1733 as a limit of binomials, decades before Gauss.
Yes, that Milton Friedman. The Friedman test came 39 years before his economics Nobel.
Half of the Radon–Nikodym derivative, a.k.a. every importance weight you've computed.
Turing's Bletchley colleague: Good–Turing smoothing, and the 1965 'intelligence explosion'.
Jelinek–Mercer smoothing, and "every time I fire a linguist, performance goes up".
The Roberts cross edge detector, 1963. Then he went off to build ARPANET.
Coined the name 'k-means' in 1967.
The Fiedler vector: the Laplacian's second eigenvector, which cuts a graph in two.
An engineer turned biostatistician. Winsorizing clips your outliers in his name.
The Woodbury identity: invert a low-rank update without inverting the whole thing. GPs say thanks.
An Austrian meteorologist. 'Hanning window' is a pun on Hamming's that stuck.
1781: move the dirt from cuttings to embankments at least total cost. Optimal transport, born.
The Lorenz attractor and the butterfly effect. Lorenz-96 is still a forecasting-ML benchmark.
The Watson in both Durbin–Watson and Nadaraya–Watson.
Chow–Liu trees, and Chow's rule for when a classifier should refuse to answer.
Tabulated the F-distribution and named it F in Fisher's honor.
Freedman–Diaconis bins. Also proved seven riffle shuffles mix a deck. Former magician.
Neal's funnel: the hierarchical-model geometry that makes HMC sad.
The Hoff in the Widrow–Hoff rule, then co-designer of the Intel 4004.
Wrote the KKT conditions in his 1939 master's thesis, 12 years before Kuhn and Tucker.
Published least squares in 1805. Gauss claimed he'd had it since 1795.
Neyman–Pearson lemma, confidence intervals, and the Neyman–Rubin potential outcomes.
The L in KL. Also an NSA cryptanalyst, like Kullback.
Chernoff bounds, and Chernoff faces: multivariate data drawn as cartoon faces.
Pioneered linear programming and relaxed Monge's transport problem. Economics Nobel, 1975.
AIC, 1973. He called it 'an information criterion'; everyone else calls it Akaike's.
Wald test, sequential analysis, and armoring the planes where returning bombers had no holes.
Tukey's HSD, box plots, the FFT with Cooley, and the words 'bit' and 'software'.
Every Hessian you've ever avoided computing is named after him.
Itô calculus: the stochastic calculus underneath every score-based diffusion SDE.
A botanist watching pollen jiggle in water, 1827. Now every diffusion model's noise source.
Hotelling's T², and the 1933 paper that gave PCA its name and its modern form.
An ecologist measuring species co-occurrence, 1945. Now a segmentation loss.
A biochemist scoring protein secondary-structure predictions, 1975. Now the MCC.
A weather forecaster. The Brier score graded rain forecasts in 1950.
Box–Cox, Box–Jenkins, Box–Muller, and "all models are wrong, but some are useful".
The MSE-optimal kernel for density estimation, and the name everyone mispronounces.
A physics professor who rated chess players. Chatbot Arena now rates LLMs his way.
Tweedie's formula: denoising is the score. Diffusion models run on a 1950s identity.
A self-taught prodigy who co-invented the artificial neuron with McCulloch in 1943.
Jordan networks, 1986. Not the basketball one, as every intro slide points out.
The Canny edge detector grew out of his MIT master's thesis. Still every OpenCV tutorial's first filter.
Huffman coding was a term paper. He picked it to skip MIT's final exam.
Lloyd's algorithm, a.k.a. k-means, written at Bell Labs in 1957 and published in 1982.
PageRank is named after Page, not web pages. Convenient.
Coined regression, correlation and the Galton board. Also eugenics, sadly.
His banana-shaped valley has humbled optimizers since 1960.
The Wasserstein distance is a transliteration of Vaserstein. Kantorovich got there first anyway.
Extreme-value statistician and anti-Nazi activist. Now powers your differentiable discrete samples.
Pareto optimality and the Pareto distribution. The 80/20 rule came from his data on land ownership.
Divide α by the number of tests. Conservative, simple, and cited constantly.
Taylor series, 1715. Every second-order optimizer starts from his expansion.
The Jacobian, the matrix of first derivatives, and the Jacobi iterative method.
Euler's method, the simplest ODE solver, which diffusion samplers build on. And e, Euler's number.
LeCun initialization (lecun_normal in Keras). The rest of his work went by other names.
The Hinton diagram: weight matrices drawn as squares sized by magnitude. matplotlib has an example.
Nash equilibria: what GAN training is supposed to find and rarely does.
A French army surveyor killed in WWI. His decomposition was published posthumously.
Hilbert spaces, home of kernel methods' RKHS, and the 23 problems he posed in 1900.
The Frobenius norm: the square root of the sum of a matrix's squared entries.
Minkowski distance, (Σ|xᵢ − yᵢ|ᵖ)^(1/p): Manhattan at p = 1, Euclidean at p = 2.
Edit distance, 1965. Every fuzzy matcher, including this game's, owes him one.
Lipschitz continuity: WGAN's critic, spectral norm, and every robustness certificate.
Laplace smoothing, the Laplace distribution, the Laplace approximation, and Bayes before Bayes caught on.
Correlation coefficient, the chi-squared test (1900) and PCA (1901). Also founded the first university statistics department.
Fisher information, Fisher's LDA, the exact test, and the iris dataset. Also the F in F-test.
Shannon entropy. His 1948 paper invented information theory more or less in one go.
Shapley values, 1953. Nobel in economics 2012, then the S in SHAP.
Probability's axioms, Kolmogorov–Smirnov, Kolmogorov complexity, and now KANs.
Chebyshev's inequality, Chebyshev polynomials and the Chebyshev (L∞) distance.
The Dirichlet distribution, LDA's prior over topic mixtures.
Lagrange multipliers: the constraint you can't escape, priced as a variable.
Newton's method for roots and optima, and half the credit for calculus.
Fourier series came out of a paper on heat flow. Now positional encodings and random features.
Euclidean distance and geometry, from his Elements, around 300 BC.
Hamming distance and Hamming codes, invented because a weekend job kept crashing on errors.
A Swiss botanist comparing plant species across Alpine districts. Now IoU.
The Huber loss, 1964: quadratic near zero, linear in the tails, robust to outliers.
The Gini coefficient of inequality, 1912. Decision trees' Gini impurity is a related but different formula.
Spearman's rank correlation (1904), and the pioneer of factor analysis.
The Turing test, Turing machines, and Good–Turing smoothing from Bletchley Park.
The Bellman equation, and the phrase 'curse of dimensionality'. He named dynamic programming to dodge a budget-hostile boss.
The Kalman filter flew on Apollo. It's still in your phone's GPS.
The Viterbi algorithm, 1967, then co-founded Qualcomm.
First name on the 1953 Metropolis algorithm paper. The Rosenbluths did most of the work.
Gibbs sampling, the Gibbs distribution, and Gibbs' inequality, which keeps KL divergence nonnegative.
Boltzmann distributions and Boltzmann machines. S = k log W is on his tombstone.
Hopfield networks, 1982. Shared the 2024 physics Nobel with Hinton.
The only researcher whose first name is a weight initializer.
He initialization, ResNet, Mask R-CNN, MoCo and MAE.
Nesterov momentum, 1983: take the gradient at the look-ahead point. The optimal rate for smooth convex problems.
Thompson sampling, 1933, for clinical trials. Forgotten for 80 years, now runs A/B tests.
The V in VC dimension, and co-inventor of the SVM.
A 14th-century friar whose razor now argues for regularization.
A Danish telephone engineer who did math on the side. Jensen's inequality, 1906.
Guinness wouldn't let him publish under his own name, so the t-test belongs to 'Student'.
The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and the Cauchy distribution. He also described gradient descent, in 1847.
Covariance-aware distance, 1936. He also founded the Indian Statistical Institute.
The K in KL. An NSA cryptanalyst who wrote Information Theory and Statistics.
A Presbyterian minister whose theorem Richard Price published two years after his death.
The Gaussian, Gauss–Newton, Gauss–Markov, Gaussian elimination. Most of a stats syllabus.
Markov chains, MDPs, Markov's inequality. First applied to vowel sequences in Pushkin's Eugene Onegin.
The Bernoulli distribution and the first law of large numbers, in Ars Conjectandi (1713).
The Poisson distribution first appeared in a book about jury verdicts.
Conceived his shortest-path algorithm in twenty minutes at a café, without pen or paper.
Chomsky hierarchy, Chomsky normal form: still the first slide of every parsing lecture.
The 1958 perceptron: a Navy-funded machine the New York Times said would one day walk, talk and be conscious.
Knuth–Morris–Pratt and the Knuth shuffle. Pays $2.56 for each error found in his books.
Bessel's correction: divide by n−1, because the sample mean sits closer to the sample than the true mean does.
Conceived Monte Carlo sampling in 1946 while wondering about his odds at solitaire.
Einstein summation: the convention behind einsum.
Bahdanau attention, 2014: the additive alignment that preceded the Transformer.
Luong attention, 2015: multiplicative scores, the dot-product ancestor of Transformer attention.
Hornik 1991: universal approximation holds for any bounded, non-constant, continuous activation.
Barron 1993: a dimension-free approximation rate for one-hidden-layer nets, for functions with bounded Fourier moment.
Oja's rule: Hebbian learning with a normalizing term that converges to the first principal component.
Natural gradient descent and information geometry.
SMART retrieval system and the vector space model, where TF-IDF grew up.
BM25: Okapi's ranking function, still the baseline dense retrievers must beat.
Invented inverse document frequency in 1972.
Distributional hypothesis, 1954: words in similar contexts have similar meanings.
"You shall know a word by the company it keeps."
Named the logistic curve in 1838 while modelling population growth.
Kabsch algorithm: the optimal rotation aligning two point sets. Protein structure's bread and butter.
Multiplied 2×2 matrices with 7 products in 1969. AlphaTensor reopened the hunt.
Newton–Schulz iteration, 1933: a matrix inverse then, Muon's orthogonalizer today.
Ferguson 1973: defined the Dirichlet process.
Holland's schema theorem and the genetic algorithm, 1975.
Bet the fraction that maximizes expected log wealth, 1956, Bell Labs.
Hurst exponent, born from measuring Nile floods.
Hydrologist whose 1980 Beta lookalike has a closed-form CDF.
Schrödinger bridges: the entropic cousin of optimal transport behind some diffusion models.
Anscombe's quartet: four datasets, identical statistics, four different pictures.
